planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall onto moist, humus-rich soil in dappled shade; seed needs a full winter of cold, moist stratification and germinates erratically over the following one to two springs.

directions: Columbian monkshood grows wild along seeps, streambanks, and moist forest margins through the montane and subalpine zones of the Rocky Mountains, often alongside aspen or spruce-fir stands where soil stays consistently damp. It sends up tall, leafy stems topped with hooded, deep blue-purple flowers in mid to late summer, giving height and vertical structure to a woodland border without needing full sun. Because every part of the plant is highly toxic if ingested and can irritate skin on contact, site it away from vegetable beds and handle divisions with gloves. Established plants resent being disturbed, so choose a permanent spot with rich, evenly moist soil and leave the crown undisturbed once it settles in.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow seed outdoors in fall and allow natural winter cold to break dormancy; seed needs light to germinate so cover only lightly with soil, and seedlings emerge the following spring in the cool, dappled light of a woodland edge or rock garden.

directions: The Colorado state flower grows naturally in the light shade of aspen groves and the open understory of spruce-fir forest from about 7,000 to 11,000 feet in elevation, where cool nights and well-drained but moisture-retentive soil keep it thriving well into summer. Long-spurred flowers in blue and white rise above gray-green, finely divided foliage from early summer onward, drawing hawkmoths and hummingbirds that can reach the nectar at the base of the spurs. It performs best in gardens that mimic its mountain habitat: morning sun or filtered light, soil that drains but never fully dries, and protection from hot afternoon exposure at lower elevations. Plants are relatively short-lived individually but self-sow readily where conditions suit them, keeping a colony going for years.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Divide spreading rhizome clumps in fall after foliage dies back and replant into humus-rich forest soil in full to partial shade; established colonies also self-sow from wind-dispersed, dandelion-like seed heads.

directions: Heartleaf arnica is one of the most abundant forest-floor wildflowers of Rocky Mountain montane and subalpine conifer stands, carpeting the ground beneath lodgepole pine, Douglas-fir, and spruce-fir canopy with heart-shaped, slightly fuzzy leaf pairs. In late spring it sends up single yellow, daisy-like flower heads on short stalks just as the surrounding forest floor is greening up after snowmelt. It spreads steadily by shallow rhizomes to form loose mats, making it a useful native substitute for non-native shade groundcovers in a woodland garden, though it goes dormant and disappears above ground for much of late summer and fall. Give it consistent but not soggy moisture and the kind of acidic, duff-covered soil found under conifers, and it will self-perpetuate with little further care.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall onto consistently moist, shaded soil near the planting site; seed requires a cold winter stratification period and germinates the following spring, with seedlings best left undisturbed for their first year.

directions: Side-flowered miterwort grows along shaded streambanks and seepy slopes within Rocky Mountain and Intermountain conifer forests, forming low rosettes of rounded, slightly hairy leaves reminiscent of a small coral bells. Its common name comes from the unusual flower arrangement: tiny, cross-shaped greenish-purple blooms are held along just one side of a slender, upright stalk rather than radiating in all directions like most of its miterwort relatives. It is a true moisture-lover best suited to the edge of a shaded rain garden, streamside planting, or the damp margin of a woodland path where it can be appreciated up close. Keep soil reliably moist and cool, and avoid locations that dry out even briefly during summer.

planting.note: Start seed indoors on the surface of a well-drained mix under bright light 6-8 weeks before the last frost; seedlings are slow to establish and should be hardened off and transplanted into rocky, fast-draining soil after frost danger passes.

directions: Rocky Mountain alumroot is a compact, drought-tolerant native of rocky slopes, cliff ledges, and open montane woods throughout the central and southern Rockies, where it roots into crevices and thin, gravelly soil pockets. It forms tidy mounds of small, rounded, lobed leaves and sends up slender, wiry flower stalks carrying tiny cream to pale pink bells in early summer that attract small bees and hummingbirds. Because it evolved on well-drained rocky sites, it is far less tolerant of soggy winter soil than larger garden Heuchera cultivars and performs best in a rock garden, dry stone wall, or gravel-mulched woodland edge. Give it morning sun or high dappled shade and resist the urge to overwater it once established.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed directly into shaded, humus-rich forest soil in fall; the bristly seed needs a period of cold, moist winter stratification and germinates sporadically over the following one to two springs.

directions: Mountain sweet cicely is a delicate, anise-scented herb of moist, shaded forest floors across the Rocky Mountains and other western ranges, where its fern-like, thrice-divided leaves blend into the duff beneath conifers and aspens. Loose, sparse umbels of small white flowers appear in late spring, followed by narrow, bristly seeds that cling to passing fur and clothing for dispersal, an unusual trait for a member of the carrot family. The crushed foliage and roots carry a mild licorice-like fragrance, and the plant was historically used in small amounts by Indigenous communities as a flavoring and minor remedy. It makes an unobtrusive filler for a shaded native herb garden but needs consistently cool, moist soil and dies back cleanly to the ground each fall.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
Native American Ethnobotany Database (University of Michigan)

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall into moist, shaded soil; seed needs a full winter of cold, moist stratification and germination is often spread across two springs rather than occurring all at once.

directions: Western meadow-rue grows in moist montane forest openings, aspen groves, and streambanks throughout the Rocky Mountains, lending an airy, fern-like texture to the shaded understory with its delicate, divided foliage. Unlike many wildflowers, individual plants are either male or female, and the male plants are the showier of the two, producing loose, dangling clusters of purple-tinged stamens in late spring while female plants bear smaller, less conspicuous flowers that mature into feathery seed heads. It spreads slowly from a fibrous rootstock and looks best massed with ferns or other woodland perennials rather than grown as a single specimen, since much of its appeal is in the overall drift of lacy foliage. Keep soil evenly moist and shaded, and avoid hot, exposed sites where the foliage scorches by midsummer.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall onto moist, acidic, duff-covered soil beneath conifers; seed needs cold winter stratification, and established plants also spread slowly by short rhizomes.

directions: Round-leaved violet is a true deep-shade specialist of Rocky Mountain montane and subalpine conifer forests, growing low against the duff beneath closed spruce-fir and lodgepole canopy where little direct light reaches the ground. Its thick, glossy, rounded leaves lie nearly flat and are often tinged purple on the underside, while small yellow flowers marked with fine purple-brown veining on the lower petal appear close to the ground just after snowmelt. It is one of the earliest forest floor plants to bloom each season, taking advantage of the brief window before the canopy fully leafs out and summer drought sets in. Because it is adapted to constant deep shade and acidic, moisture-retentive soil, it struggles in beds that get much direct sun and is best reserved for the darkest corner of a conifer-shaded native garden.

planting.note: Take hardwood cuttings in late fall after leaf drop and root in a shaded cold frame, or transplant container-grown nursery stock in fall into moist, humus-rich soil at the edge of forest cover.

directions: Wolf's currant is an unarmed, spineless shrub of the central and northern Rocky Mountains, growing in the dappled shade of montane conifer forest understory and along shaded forest margins rather than in open ground. Small yellowish, tubular flowers appear in loose clusters in spring, followed by purplish-black berries that ripen in late summer and are readily eaten by birds, bears, and other wildlife, while deer and elk browse the foliage and stems. Unlike many of its prickly gooseberry relatives, it has smooth stems that make it easier to work around in a mixed woodland planting, and it tolerates a range of soil types as long as moisture is adequate. It is most useful as a wildlife-supporting backbone shrub in a native woodland or restoration planting rather than as a showy ornamental specimen.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
Native American Ethnobotany Database (University of Michigan)
